body: I'd like to suggest using `inline` for loops too, it's intuitive enough, [there is precedent](https://ziglang.org/documentation/master/#inline-for), and one new keyword is better than two new keywords.

> I'd like to suggest using inline for loops too, it's intuitive enough, [there is precedent](https://ziglang.org/documentation/master/#inline-for), and one new keyword is better than two new keywords.

I'm open to other suggestions, but that naming from zig is very bad imo (not just neutral, it's actively bad naming).
It's not an inline. You can have unrolling without inlining, or inlining without unrolling.

I've personally come to the opinion that although naming is one of the more difficult concepts, we should name things based on *what they are*, and not on *what they are not*. This has managed to trip us up a few times in the past.

Grok suggests it's a historical anomaly in zig based on how they did this optimization in their particular implementation.

> Yes, calling loop unrolling "unroll" instead of "inline" in Zig would likely be more intuitive and precise, as the two terms—unrolling and inlining—refer to distinct compiler optimizations, even though they share some conceptual overlap. Here’s a concise breakdown of why "unroll" might be a better name and the nuances involved:
> ### Distinct Concepts:
> * Loop Unrolling: This is the process of expanding a loop’s iterations into a sequence of repeated statements to reduce loop overhead and enable further optimizations. For example, a loop with three iterations might be transformed into three explicit statements.
> * Inlining: This typically refers to replacing a function call with the function’s body to eliminate call overhead. While inlining can sometimes lead to opportunities for loop unrolling within the inlined code, the two are not identical.
>
> Using "inline" for loop unrolling can blur these distinctions, potentially confusing developers familiar with standard compiler terminology where "unrolling" is the established term for this optimization.

We would be better off discussing this on RocketChat but I'm in the opinion that using two separate keywords for roughly the same goal may become confusing.

It still doesn't help that the optimizations both of these keywords provide are, for the most part, not perceivable to beginners or common GDScript users; in general both keywords don't change anything on the outside, and for simple use-cases it's better to have them than not.
###### What if you have to opt-out of optimizations instead?

I wonder if we could have an unique keyword that makes their purpose more obvious. Something along the lines of `optimized`.

Pinging for any reviews, this may be a little late for 3.7 dev 1 but it would be nice to get ball rolling regarding any changes still desired here (maybe in terms of architecture or whatever that I might not have thought of).

Great feedback!

> The optimization options on GDScript resources are lost when the scene is reloaded, since a GDScript file can't store metadata. This means they don't affect the runtime at all, since running the project implies reloading the scene somehow.

Ah that's a pain, I was assuming they were being serialized. I'll look into it. :+1: 

> This function is considered not inlinable by the optimizer:

Recursive functions are exlicitly not inlined (they are pretty tricky to in sensible ways in general), but in this case this particular sequence of returns may not be supported (it's quite complex to support return statements under the hood because GDScript has no `goto` function), and that problem is probably flagged before the recursion.

I'll try and take a look at the points in detail later.
